sermons.life_context: He was president of Northwestern Schools in Minneapolis (from 1948) and a vice president of Youth for Christ International, with his family based in Montreat, North Carolina. This opening meeting began the campaign that first brought him national media attention; the BGEA was incorporated a year later.

He was about two months into the 16-week New York Crusade (15 May–1 September 1957), whose Madison Square Garden meetings ABC had broadcast live on several nights since June. He led the BGEA, incorporated in 1950, having left the Northwestern Schools presidency in 1952; home was Montreat, North Carolina, where he and Ruth had four children, with a fifth, Ned, born in 1958.

Home was Montreat, North Carolina, where he and Ruth had five children, the youngest born in 1958, and he was holding crusades around the world. Eleven years earlier, at his 1953 Chattanooga crusade, described as his first integrated one, he had refused to let ushers put back ropes segregating Black listeners.
Based at Montreat, North Carolina, he was holding crusades around the world, and The Hour of Decision, the BGEA's weekly radio programme, had been on the air since November 1950.
Based at Montreat, North Carolina, where he and Ruth had five children, the youngest, Ned, born in 1958, he was holding crusades around the world.
Based at Montreat, North Carolina, he was holding crusades around the world; six months earlier he had closed the Seoul crusade at Yoido Plaza.

Based at Montreat, North Carolina, he was holding crusades around the world, a ministry that had reached communist Eastern Europe with his 1977 visit to Hungary. In May 1982 he had addressed a Soviet-sponsored religious peace conference in Moscow, where his reported remark that there was "a measure of religious freedom" drew Western criticism.

Based at Montreat, North Carolina, he was still holding crusades around the world. Since 1977 he had also preached in communist Eastern Europe, and in 1982 he had addressed a Soviet-sponsored religious peace conference in Moscow.

Still based at Montreat and holding crusades, he was in the year his illness became public: in July 1992 his spokesman announced he had been in the early stages of Parkinson's disease for three years, with mild tremors and some difficulty walking. He also visited North Korea in 1992.

Based at Montreat, North Carolina, he kept holding crusades after his spokesman announced in July 1992 that he had been in the early stages of Parkinson's disease for three years. He had visited North Korea in 1992.

Based at Montreat, North Carolina, he was in the final phase of his crusade ministry and had kept preaching since his Parkinson's disease was announced in July 1992; the previous year, 1994, he had made his second visit to North Korea.

Still based at Montreat, North Carolina, he had kept preaching since his Parkinson's disease was announced in 1992, while handing over the BGEA: his son Franklin became its chief executive officer in 2000 and its president in 2001.
He came to New York using a walker, living with Parkinson's disease and prostate cancer, and had handed leadership of the BGEA to his son Franklin in 2000–01. Home remained Montreat, North Carolina.

Retired at Montreat, North Carolina, he had made only a few public appearances since 2005, including New Orleans in March 2006. His wife Ruth had died at their home there in June 2007, weeks after the Billy Graham Library in Charlotte was dedicated; this was his last televised message.
